children.proof_nl:
Work in the formal power series ring Z[[q]]. Since 0 <= a <= b and r >= 0, all indices occurring in the q-Pochhammer symbols are nonnegative, so the definitions make sense.

First rewrite the rational function R_{a,b,r}(q). Because a <= b, we have
(q;q)_{r+b}/(q;q)_{r+a} = (\prod_{t=1}^{r+b} (1-q^t))/(\prod_{t=1}^{r+a} (1-q^t)) = \prod_{t=r+a+1}^{r+b} (1-q^t).
Reindexing with t = r+i gives
(q;q)_{r+b}/(q;q)_{r+a} = \prod_{i=a+1}^{b} (1-q^{r+i}).
Also,
(q;q)_a/(q;q)_b = (\prod_{t=1}^{a} (1-q^t))/(\prod_{t=1}^{b} (1-q^t)) = 1/\prod_{t=a+1}^{b} (1-q^t).
Therefore
R_{a,b,r}(q) = \prod_{i=a+1}^{b} \frac{1-q^{r+i}}{1-q^i}.
When a=b, these are empty products and equal 1, so the same formula is still valid.

Now fix an integer i >= 1. In Z[[q]] one has
(1-q^i) \sum_{m>=0} q^{mi} = \sum_{m>=0} q^{mi} - \sum_{m>=0} q^{(m+1)i} = 1,
because the coefficient of q^0 is 1 and for every positive multiple ni of i the two sums contribute equally and cancel. Hence
(1-q^i)^{-1} = \sum_{m>=0} q^{mi}
inside Z[[q]].

Substituting this inverse into the product formula for R_{a,b,r}(q), and using that the product over i is finite, we obtain in Z[[q]]:
R_{a,b,r}(q) = \prod_{i=a+1}^{b} (1-q^{r+i})(1-q^i)^{-1}
= \prod_{i=a+1}^{b} \left((1-q^{r+i}) \sum_{m>=0} q^{mi}\right)
= F_{a,b,r}(q).
Thus F_{a,b,r}(q) is exactly the formal power-series expansion at q=0 of the rational function R_{a,b,r}(q).

For the final claim, assume R_{a,b,r}(q) belongs to Z[q]. A polynomial, viewed as an element of Z[[q]], is equal to its own power-series expansion at q=0 (with all coefficients above its degree equal to 0). Since the expansion of R_{a,b,r}(q) is F_{a,b,r}(q), we have equality of formal power series
R_{a,b,r}(q) = F_{a,b,r}(q)
in Z[[q]]. Therefore, for every integer j >= 0, the coefficients of q^j are equal:
[q^j] R_{a,b,r}(q) = [q^j] F_{a,b,r}(q).
This proves the lemma.

children.proof_nl:
Let e_d := M_d(r+a,r+b) - M_d(a,b) for each positive integer d. First rewrite the quotient of q-Pochhammer symbols. Since a <= b and r >= 0, we have (q;q)_{r+b}/(q;q)_{r+a} = product_{t=r+a+1}^{r+b} (1 - q^t) and (q;q)_a/(q;q)_b = 1 / product_{t=a+1}^{b} (1 - q^t). Therefore
R_{a,b,r}(q) = product_{i=a+1}^{b} (1 - q^{r+i})/(1 - q^i),
with the empty product equal to 1 when a=b.

Now use the defining factorization of cyclotomic polynomials: for every positive integer N,
q^N - 1 = product_{d | N} Phi_d(q).
For each i with a+1 <= i <= b,
(1 - q^{r+i})/(1 - q^i) = (q^{r+i} - 1)/(q^i - 1) = (product_{d | (r+i)} Phi_d(q)) / (product_{d | i} Phi_d(q)).
Multiplying over i from a+1 to b and collecting equal cyclotomic factors, we get an identity of rational functions
R_{a,b,r}(q) = product_{d >= 1} Phi_d(q)^(A_d - B_d),
where
A_d := |{ i in Z : a < i <= b and d divides (r+i) }|,
B_d := |{ i in Z : a < i <= b and d divides i }|.
If d > r+b, then necessarily d > b as well, so both A_d and B_d are 0. Hence only finitely many exponents are nonzero, so this product is well defined.

It remains to identify A_d and B_d with the M_d counts. The map i -> m := r+i is a bijection from the set counted by A_d onto the set { m in Z : r+a < m <= r+b and d divides m }. Therefore A_d = M_d(r+a,r+b). Also, by definition, B_d = M_d(a,b). Substituting these equalities gives
R_{a,b,r}(q) = product_{d >= 1} Phi_d(q)^( M_d(r+a,r+b) - M_d(a,b) ),
which is the claimed cyclotomic factorization.

For the consequence, assume that R_{a,b,r}(q) belongs to Z[q]. Let I_+ := { d >= 1 : e_d > 0 } and I_- := { d >= 1 : e_d < 0 }. These sets are finite because e_d = 0 for d > r+b. The factorization above can then be written as
R_{a,b,r}(q) = (product_{d in I_+} Phi_d(q)^{e_d}) / (product_{d in I_-} Phi_d(q)^{-e_d}).
Suppose, for contradiction, that I_- is nonempty. Choose D in I_-. Since R_{a,b,r}(q) is actually a polynomial, say P(q) in Z[q], clearing denominators yields the polynomial identity over C,
P(q) product_{d in I_-} Phi_d(q)^{-e_d} = product_{d in I_+} Phi_d(q)^{e_d}.
Now let zeta be a primitive D-th root of unity. By the defining root property of cyclotomic polynomials, Phi_D(zeta)=0, and for every d != D one has Phi_d(zeta) != 0 because zeta is not a primitive d-th root of unity. Evaluating the cleared polynomial identity at q=zeta, the left-hand side is 0 because it contains the factor Phi_D(zeta)^{-e_D} with -e_D > 0, while the right-hand side is nonzero because none of its factors vanish at zeta. This contradiction shows that I_- must be empty.

Thus e_d >= 0 for every positive integer d, i.e.
M_d(r+a,r+b) >= M_d(a,b)
for every positive integer d. This is exactly the stated consequence.

children.proof_nl:
Let I = {a+1, a+2, ..., b}. Fix j >= 0. Since a >= 0, every i in I is a positive integer. Hence any term q^(m i) with m > floor(j/i) has degree greater than j, so it cannot contribute to the coefficient of q^j in a product whose other factors also have only nonnegative exponents. Therefore
[q^j] F_{a,b,r}(q) = [q^j] product_{i in I} ((1 - q^(r+i)) sum_{m=0}^{floor(j/i)} q^(m i)).
The right-hand side is now the coefficient of a finite product of finite sums, so we may expand it by the ordinary distributive law.

For each i in I, write
(1 - q^(r+i)) sum_{m=0}^{floor(j/i)} q^(m i) = (sum_{m=0}^{floor(j/i)} q^(m i)) + (- q^(r+i) sum_{m=0}^{floor(j/i)} q^(m i)).
In the full expansion of the product, choose the second bracket exactly for those i belonging to some subset S of I. For each i, also choose one integer m_i >= 0 from the geometric sum. The resulting monomial is then
(-1)^(|S|) q^( sum_{i in I} m_i i + sum_{s in S} (r+s) ).
Hence
[q^j] F_{a,b,r}(q) = sum over all subsets S of I of sum over all families (m_i)_{i in I} of nonnegative integers satisfying sum_{i in I} m_i i + sum_{s in S}(r+s) = j of (-1)^(|S|).
(The bounds m_i <= floor(j/i) are automatic from the displayed equation, so they do not need to be written separately.)

Now such a family (m_i)_{i in I} is the same thing as a finite multiset lambda of elements of I: namely, lambda contains exactly m_i copies of i for each i in I. Conversely, every finite multiset of elements of I gives such a family of multiplicities. Under this bijection,
|lambda| = sum_{i in I} i m_i.
Therefore, for each fixed S, the inner sum is exactly over those finite multisets lambda of elements of I such that
|lambda| + sum_{s in S}(r+s) = j.
So we get
[q^j] F_{a,b,r}(q) = sum over all subsets S of I of sum over all finite multisets lambda of elements of I with |lambda| + sum_{s in S}(r+s) = j of (-1)^(|S|).
By the definition of X_j, this is exactly
sum_{(S,lambda) in X_j} (-1)^(|S|).
Thus [q^j] F_{a,b,r}(q) = sum_{(S,lambda) in X_j} (-1)^(|S|), as claimed.

Finally, the sum over X_j is finite: if (S,lambda) belongs to X_j, then |lambda| <= j, and since every element of I is at least 1, lambda has at most j elements. Because I is finite, there are only finitely many such multisets lambda, and there are only finitely many subsets S of I. So the right-hand side is well-defined.

children.proof_nl:
Let F := {x in X : iota(x) = x} be the set of fixed points, and let M := X \ F. Since X is finite, both F and M are finite, and X is the disjoint union F ⊔ M. Therefore
sum_{x in X} w(x) = sum_{x in F} w(x) + sum_{x in M} w(x).

First consider F. By hypothesis, whenever iota(x) = x we have w(x) = +1. Hence every term in the sum over F equals 1, so
sum_{x in F} w(x) = |F|.

Now consider M. If x belongs to M, then iota(x) != x. Also iota(iota(x)) = x, so iota(x) is again in M; thus each x in M belongs to a two-element set {x, iota(x)}. Let
O := { {x, iota(x)} : x in M }.
Each member of O has exactly two elements, because x != iota(x) for x in M. Moreover, O is a partition of M: every x in M lies in {x, iota(x)}, and if two such sets intersect, then they are equal. Indeed, if z lies in both {x, iota(x)} and {y, iota(y)}, then {x, iota(x)} = {z, iota(z)} and also {y, iota(y)} = {z, iota(z)}, so the two sets are equal.

Since O partitions M, we may sum over its blocks:
sum_{x in M} w(x) = sum_{A in O} sum_{x in A} w(x).
For any block A in O, write A = {x, iota(x)} with x in M. Then iota(x) != x, so the sign-reversal hypothesis applies and gives w(iota(x)) = -w(x). Therefore
sum_{y in A} w(y) = w(x) + w(iota(x)) = w(x) - w(x) = 0.
Thus every block contributes 0, and consequently
sum_{x in M} w(x) = 0.

Combining the two parts,
sum_{x in X} w(x) = |F| + 0 = |F| = |{x in X : iota(x) = x}|.
This proves the stated identity. In particular, the sum is the cardinality of a finite set, hence a nonnegative integer.

children.proof_nl:
Let
Q(q) := product_{i=a+1}^b ((1 - q^(r+i)) / (1 - q^i)).
For the fixed j, write
E_j := { (S, lambda) in X_j : |S| is even }
and
O_j := { (S, lambda) in X_j : |S| is odd }.
Because I is finite and every element of I is a positive integer, there are only finitely many multisets lambda with |lambda| <= j; hence X_j, E_j, and O_j are finite.

First, the coefficient of q^j in Q(q) is exactly |E_j| - |O_j|. Indeed, for each i in I,
(1 - q^(r+i)) / (1 - q^i) = (1 - q^(r+i)) * sum_{m>=0} q^(mi).
When we expand the whole product, choosing the term -q^(r+i) from the numerator factor means that i is placed into S, while choosing q^(mi) from the geometric-series factor means that lambda contains i with multiplicity m. The total exponent is then
sum_{s in S} (r+s) + |lambda|,
and the sign is (-1)^|S|. Therefore the coefficient of q^j is
sum_{(S,lambda) in X_j} (-1)^|S| = |E_j| - |O_j|.

Next, Q(q) is a polynomial. Using the cyclotomic factorization 1 - q^m = product_{d|m} Phi_d(q), the exponent of Phi_d(q) in Q(q) is
|{ i in I : d divides (r+i) }| - |{ i in I : d divides i }|.
Since I = {a+1,...,b}, this exponent is exactly
M_d(r+a,r+b) - M_d(a,b),
which is >= 0 by hypothesis. Hence every cyclotomic exponent in Q(q) is nonnegative, so Q(q) belongs to Z[q].

Now set N := r + a + b. By the standard product formula for Gaussian q-binomial coefficients,
[N choose k]_q = (q;q)_N / ((q;q)_k (q;q)_(N-k)).
Therefore
[N choose b]_q / [N choose a]_q
= ((q;q)_a (q;q)_(N-a)) / ((q;q)_b (q;q)_(N-b))
= ((q;q)_a (q;q)_(r+b)) / ((q;q)_b (q;q)_(r+a))

We have just shown that this quotient is a polynomial. Applying the allowed Gaussian-quotient positivity statement with n = N, k = b, and l = a, it follows that every coefficient of Q(q) is nonnegative. In particular, the coefficient of q^j is nonnegative. By the first paragraph, this says
|E_j| - |O_j| >= 0,

Since E_j and O_j are finite and |E_j| >= |O_j|, choose an injection f : O_j -> E_j. Define iota_j : X_j -> X_j by

- if x is in the image f(O_j), set iota_j(x) := f^{-1}(x);
- if x in E_j \ f(O_j), set iota_j(x) := x.
This is well-defined because f is injective, and clearly iota_j^2 = id_{X_j}; so iota_j is an involution.

If iota_j(S,lambda) = (S',lambda') != (S,lambda), then one of the two elements lies in O_j and the other lies in E_j, so |S'| and |S| have opposite parity. Equivalently,
|S'| ≡ |S| + 1 mod 2.
If iota_j(S,lambda) = (S,lambda), then (S,lambda) lies in E_j, so |S| is even.

Thus there exists an involution iota_j : X_j -> X_j with properties (1) and (2).

1. lem_20260329105843_95b318e7: Let a, b, r be integers with 0 <= a <= b and r >= 0. Define (q;q)_0 := 1 and (q;q)_n := product_{t=1}^n (1 - q^t) for n >= 1. Define the rational function R_{a,b,r}(q) := ((q;q)_{r+b} (q;q)_a) / ((q;q)_{r+a} (q;q)_b). Also define the formal power series F_{a,b,r}(q) := product_{i=a+1}^b ((1 - q^(r+i)) * sum_{m>=0} q^(m i)). Then F_{a,b,r}(q) is the power-series expansion at q = 0 of the rational function R_{a,b,r}(q). In particular, if R_{a,b,r}(q) belongs to Z[q], then for every integer j >= 0 one has [q^j] R_{a,b,r}(q) = [q^j] F_{a,b,r}(q).
Work in the formal power series ring Z[[q]]. Since 0 <= a <= b and r >= 0, all indices occurring in the q-Pochhammer symbols are nonnegative, so the definitions make sense.

First rewrite the rational function R_{a,b,r}(q). Because a <= b, we have
(q;q)_{r+b}/(q;q)_{r+a} = (\prod_{t=1}^{r+b} (1-q^t))/(\prod_{t=1}^{r+a} (1-q^t)) = \prod_{t=r+a+1}^{r+b} (1-q^t).
Reindexing with t = r+i gives
(q;q)_{r+b}/(q;q)_{r+a} = \prod_{i=a+1}^{b} (1-q^{r+i}).
Also,
(q;q)_a/(q;q)_b = (\prod_{t=1}^{a} (1-q^t))/(\prod_{t=1}^{b} (1-q^t)) = 1/\prod_{t=a+1}^{b} (1-q^t).
Therefore
R_{a,b,r}(q) = \prod_{i=a+1}^{b} \frac{1-q^{r+i}}{1-q^i}.
When a=b, these are empty products and equal 1, so the same formula is still valid.

Now fix an integer i >= 1. In Z[[q]] one has
(1-q^i) \sum_{m>=0} q^{mi} = \sum_{m>=0} q^{mi} - \sum_{m>=0} q^{(m+1)i} = 1,
because the coefficient of q^0 is 1 and for every positive multiple ni of i the two sums contribute equally and cancel. Hence
(1-q^i)^{-1} = \sum_{m>=0} q^{mi}
inside Z[[q]].

Substituting this inverse into the product formula for R_{a,b,r}(q), and using that the product over i is finite, we obtain in Z[[q]]:
R_{a,b,r}(q) = \prod_{i=a+1}^{b} (1-q^{r+i})(1-q^i)^{-1}
= \prod_{i=a+1}^{b} \left((1-q^{r+i}) \sum_{m>=0} q^{mi}\right)
= F_{a,b,r}(q).
Thus F_{a,b,r}(q) is exactly the formal power-series expansion at q=0 of the rational function R_{a,b,r}(q).

For the final claim, assume R_{a,b,r}(q) belongs to Z[q]. A polynomial, viewed as an element of Z[[q]], is equal to its own power-series expansion at q=0 (with all coefficients above its degree equal to 0). Since the expansion of R_{a,b,r}(q) is F_{a,b,r}(q), we have equality of formal power series
R_{a,b,r}(q) = F_{a,b,r}(q)
in Z[[q]]. Therefore, for every integer j >= 0, the coefficients of q^j are equal:
[q^j] R_{a,b,r}(q) = [q^j] F_{a,b,r}(q).
This proves the lemma.

2. lem_20260329105900_ed0a9993: Let a, b, r be integers with 0 <= a <= b and r >= 0. Define (q;q)_0 := 1 and (q;q)_n := product_{t=1}^n (1 - q^t) for n >= 1, and define R_{a,b,r}(q) := ((q;q)_{r+b} (q;q)_a) / ((q;q)_{r+a} (q;q)_b). For each positive integer d, define M_d(u,v) := |{m in Z : u < m <= v and d divides m}|. Then one has the cyclotomic factorization R_{a,b,r}(q) = product_{d>=1} Phi_d(q)^( M_d(r+a,r+b) - M_d(a,b) ), where Phi_d(q) is the d-th cyclotomic polynomial. Consequently, if R_{a,b,r}(q) belongs to Z[q], then M_d(r+a,r+b) >= M_d(a,b) for every positive integer d.
Let e_d := M_d(r+a,r+b) - M_d(a,b) for each positive integer d. First rewrite the quotient of q-Pochhammer symbols. Since a <= b and r >= 0, we have (q;q)_{r+b}/(q;q)_{r+a} = product_{t=r+a+1}^{r+b} (1 - q^t) and (q;q)_a/(q;q)_b = 1 / product_{t=a+1}^{b} (1 - q^t). Therefore
R_{a,b,r}(q) = product_{i=a+1}^{b} (1 - q^{r+i})/(1 - q^i),
with the empty product equal to 1 when a=b.

Now use the defining factorization of cyclotomic polynomials: for every positive integer N,
q^N - 1 = product_{d | N} Phi_d(q).
For each i with a+1 <= i <= b,
(1 - q^{r+i})/(1 - q^i) = (q^{r+i} - 1)/(q^i - 1) = (product_{d | (r+i)} Phi_d(q)) / (product_{d | i} Phi_d(q)).
Multiplying over i from a+1 to b and collecting equal cyclotomic factors, we get an identity of rational functions
R_{a,b,r}(q) = product_{d >= 1} Phi_d(q)^(A_d - B_d),
where
A_d := |{ i in Z : a < i <= b and d divides (r+i) }|,
B_d := |{ i in Z : a < i <= b and d divides i }|.
If d > r+b, then necessarily d > b as well, so both A_d and B_d are 0. Hence only finitely many exponents are nonzero, so this product is well defined.

It remains to identify A_d and B_d with the M_d counts. The map i -> m := r+i is a bijection from the set counted by A_d onto the set { m in Z : r+a < m <= r+b and d divides m }. Therefore A_d = M_d(r+a,r+b). Also, by definition, B_d = M_d(a,b). Substituting these equalities gives
R_{a,b,r}(q) = product_{d >= 1} Phi_d(q)^( M_d(r+a,r+b) - M_d(a,b) ),
which is the claimed cyclotomic factorization.

For the consequence, assume that R_{a,b,r}(q) belongs to Z[q]. Let I_+ := { d >= 1 : e_d > 0 } and I_- := { d >= 1 : e_d < 0 }. These sets are finite because e_d = 0 for d > r+b. The factorization above can then be written as
R_{a,b,r}(q) = (product_{d in I_+} Phi_d(q)^{e_d}) / (product_{d in I_-} Phi_d(q)^{-e_d}).
Suppose, for contradiction, that I_- is nonempty. Choose D in I_-. Since R_{a,b,r}(q) is actually a polynomial, say P(q) in Z[q], clearing denominators yields the polynomial identity over C,
P(q) product_{d in I_-} Phi_d(q)^{-e_d} = product_{d in I_+} Phi_d(q)^{e_d}.
Now let zeta be a primitive D-th root of unity. By the defining root property of cyclotomic polynomials, Phi_D(zeta)=0, and for every d != D one has Phi_d(zeta) != 0 because zeta is not a primitive d-th root of unity. Evaluating the cleared polynomial identity at q=zeta, the left-hand side is 0 because it contains the factor Phi_D(zeta)^{-e_D} with -e_D > 0, while the right-hand side is nonzero because none of its factors vanish at zeta. This contradiction shows that I_- must be empty.

Thus e_d >= 0 for every positive integer d, i.e.
M_d(r+a,r+b) >= M_d(a,b)
for every positive integer d. This is exactly the stated consequence.

3. lem_20260329105924_711791c7: Let a, b, r, j be integers with 0 <= a <= b, r >= 0, and j >= 0. Put I := {a+1, a+2, ..., b}. Define the formal power series F_{a,b,r}(q) := product_{i in I} ((1 - q^(r+i)) * sum_{m>=0} q^(m i)). Let X_j be the set of pairs (S, lambda) such that S is a subset of I, lambda is a finite multiset of elements of I, |lambda| denotes the sum of the elements of lambda, and |lambda| + sum_{s in S} (r + s) = j. Then [q^j] F_{a,b,r}(q) = sum_{(S,lambda) in X_j} (-1)^(|S|).
Let I = {a+1, a+2, ..., b}. Fix j >= 0. Since a >= 0, every i in I is a positive integer. Hence any term q^(m i) with m > floor(j/i) has degree greater than j, so it cannot contribute to the coefficient of q^j in a product whose other factors also have only nonnegative exponents. Therefore
[q^j] F_{a,b,r}(q) = [q^j] product_{i in I} ((1 - q^(r+i)) sum_{m=0}^{floor(j/i)} q^(m i)).
The right-hand side is now the coefficient of a finite product of finite sums, so we may expand it by the ordinary distributive law.

For each i in I, write
(1 - q^(r+i)) sum_{m=0}^{floor(j/i)} q^(m i) = (sum_{m=0}^{floor(j/i)} q^(m i)) + (- q^(r+i) sum_{m=0}^{floor(j/i)} q^(m i)).
In the full expansion of the product, choose the second bracket exactly for those i belonging to some subset S of I. For each i, also choose one integer m_i >= 0 from the geometric sum. The resulting monomial is then
(-1)^(|S|) q^( sum_{i in I} m_i i + sum_{s in S} (r+s) ).
Hence
[q^j] F_{a,b,r}(q) = sum over all subsets S of I of sum over all families (m_i)_{i in I} of nonnegative integers satisfying sum_{i in I} m_i i + sum_{s in S}(r+s) = j of (-1)^(|S|).
(The bounds m_i <= floor(j/i) are automatic from the displayed equation, so they do not need to be written separately.)

Now such a family (m_i)_{i in I} is the same thing as a finite multiset lambda of elements of I: namely, lambda contains exactly m_i copies of i for each i in I. Conversely, every finite multiset of elements of I gives such a family of multiplicities. Under this bijection,
|lambda| = sum_{i in I} i m_i.
Therefore, for each fixed S, the inner sum is exactly over those finite multisets lambda of elements of I such that
|lambda| + sum_{s in S}(r+s) = j.
So we get
[q^j] F_{a,b,r}(q) = sum over all subsets S of I of sum over all finite multisets lambda of elements of I with |lambda| + sum_{s in S}(r+s) = j of (-1)^(|S|).
By the definition of X_j, this is exactly
sum_{(S,lambda) in X_j} (-1)^(|S|).
Thus [q^j] F_{a,b,r}(q) = sum_{(S,lambda) in X_j} (-1)^(|S|), as claimed.

Finally, the sum over X_j is finite: if (S,lambda) belongs to X_j, then |lambda| <= j, and since every element of I is at least 1, lambda has at most j elements. Because I is finite, there are only finitely many such multisets lambda, and there are only finitely many subsets S of I. So the right-hand side is well-defined.

4. lem_20260329105947_d7a87760: Let X be a finite set and let w : X -> { -1, +1 } be a sign function. Suppose iota : X -> X satisfies iota(iota(x)) = x for every x in X, w(iota(x)) = -w(x) whenever iota(x) != x, and w(x) = +1 whenever iota(x) = x. Then sum_{x in X} w(x) = |{x in X : iota(x) = x}|. In particular, sum_{x in X} w(x) is a nonnegative integer.
Let F := {x in X : iota(x) = x} be the set of fixed points, and let M := X \ F. Since X is finite, both F and M are finite, and X is the disjoint union F ⊔ M. Therefore
sum_{x in X} w(x) = sum_{x in F} w(x) + sum_{x in M} w(x).

First consider F. By hypothesis, whenever iota(x) = x we have w(x) = +1. Hence every term in the sum over F equals 1, so
sum_{x in F} w(x) = |F|.

Now consider M. If x belongs to M, then iota(x) != x. Also iota(iota(x)) = x, so iota(x) is again in M; thus each x in M belongs to a two-element set {x, iota(x)}. Let
O := { {x, iota(x)} : x in M }.
Each member of O has exactly two elements, because x != iota(x) for x in M. Moreover, O is a partition of M: every x in M lies in {x, iota(x)}, and if two such sets intersect, then they are equal. Indeed, if z lies in both {x, iota(x)} and {y, iota(y)}, then {x, iota(x)} = {z, iota(z)} and also {y, iota(y)} = {z, iota(z)}, so the two sets are equal.

Since O partitions M, we may sum over its blocks:
sum_{x in M} w(x) = sum_{A in O} sum_{x in A} w(x).
For any block A in O, write A = {x, iota(x)} with x in M. Then iota(x) != x, so the sign-reversal hypothesis applies and gives w(iota(x)) = -w(x). Therefore
sum_{y in A} w(y) = w(x) + w(iota(x)) = w(x) - w(x) = 0.
Thus every block contributes 0, and consequently
sum_{x in M} w(x) = 0.

Combining the two parts,
sum_{x in X} w(x) = |F| + 0 = |F| = |{x in X : iota(x) = x}|.
This proves the stated identity. In particular, the sum is the cardinality of a finite set, hence a nonnegative integer.

5. lem_20260329110006_654a633e: Let a, b, r, j be integers with 0 <= a <= b, r >= 0, and 0 <= j <= floor(r (b - a) / 2). Put I := {a+1, a+2, ..., b}. For each positive integer d, define M_d(u,v) := |{m in Z : u < m <= v and d divides m}|, and assume M_d(r+a,r+b) >= M_d(a,b) for every positive integer d. Then there exists an involution iota_j : X_j -> X_j such that: (1) if iota_j(S,lambda) = (S',lambda') != (S,lambda), then |S'| is congruent to |S| + 1 modulo 2; and (2) if iota_j(S,lambda) = (S,lambda), then |S| is even.

Q(q) := product_{i=a+1}^b ((1 - q^(r+i)) / (1 - q^i)).
For the fixed j, write
E_j := { (S, lambda) in X_j : |S| is even }
and
O_j := { (S, lambda) in X_j : |S| is odd }.
Because I is finite and every element of I is a positive integer, there are only finitely many multisets lambda with |lambda| <= j; hence X_j, E_j, and O_j are finite.

First, the coefficient of q^j in Q(q) is exactly |E_j| - |O_j|. Indeed, for each i in I,
(1 - q^(r+i)) / (1 - q^i) = (1 - q^(r+i)) * sum_{m>=0} q^(mi).
When we expand the whole product, choosing the term -q^(r+i) from the numerator factor means that i is placed into S, while choosing q^(mi) from the geometric-series factor means that lambda contains i with multiplicity m. The total exponent is then
sum_{s in S} (r+s) + |lambda|,
and the sign is (-1)^|S|. Therefore the coefficient of q^j is
sum_{(S,lambda) in X_j} (-1)^|S| = |E_j| - |O_j|.

Next, Q(q) is a polynomial. Using the cyclotomic factorization 1 - q^m = product_{d|m} Phi_d(q), the exponent of Phi_d(q) in Q(q) is

Since I = {a+1,...,b}, this exponent is exactly
M_d(r+a,r+b) - M_d(a,b),
which is >= 0 by hypothesis. Hence every cyclotomic exponent in Q(q) is nonnegative, so Q(q) belongs to Z[q].

Now set N := r + a + b. By the standard product formula for Gaussian q-binomial coefficients,
[N choose k]_q = (q;q)_N / ((q;q)_k (q;q)_(N-k)).
Therefore
[N choose b]_q / [N choose a]_q
= ((q;q)_a (q;q)_(N-a)) / ((q;q)_b (q;q)_(N-b))
= ((q;q)_a (q;q)_(r+b)) / ((q;q)_b (q;q)_(r+a))
= Q(q),
because N-a = r+b and N-b = r+a.

We have just shown that this quotient is a polynomial. Applying the allowed Gaussian-quotient positivity statement with n = N, k = b, and l = a, it follows that every coefficient of Q(q) is nonnegative. In particular, the coefficient of q^j is nonnegative. By the first paragraph, this says
|E_j| - |O_j| >= 0,
so |E_j| >= |O_j|.

Since E_j and O_j are finite and |E_j| >= |O_j|, choose an injection f : O_j -> E_j. Define iota_j : X_j -> X_j by
- if x in O_j, set iota_j(x) := f(x);
- if x is in the image f(O_j), set iota_j(x) := f^{-1}(x);
- if x in E_j \ f(O_j), set iota_j(x) := x.
This is well-defined because f is injective, and clearly iota_j^2 = id_{X_j}; so iota_j is an involution.

If iota_j(S,lambda) = (S',lambda') != (S,lambda), then one of the two elements lies in O_j and the other lies in E_j, so |S'| and |S| have opposite parity. Equivalently,
|S'| ≡ |S| + 1 mod 2.
If iota_j(S,lambda) = (S,lambda), then (S,lambda) lies in E_j, so |S| is even.

Thus there exists an involution iota_j : X_j -> X_j with properties (1) and (2).

1. lem_20260329105843_95b318e7: Let a, b, r be integers with 0 <= a <= b and r >= 0. Define (q;q)_0 := 1 and (q;q)_n := product_{t=1}^n (1 - q^t) for n >= 1. Define the rational function R_{a,b,r}(q) := ((q;q)_{r+b} (q;q)_a) / ((q;q)_{r+a} (q;q)_b). Also define the formal power series F_{a,b,r}(q) := product_{i=a+1}^b ((1 - q^(r+i)) * sum_{m>=0} q^(m i)). Then F_{a,b,r}(q) is the power-series expansion at q = 0 of the rational function R_{a,b,r}(q). In particular, if R_{a,b,r}(q) belongs to Z[q], then for every integer j >= 0 one has [q^j] R_{a,b,r}(q) = [q^j] F_{a,b,r}(q).
Work in the formal power series ring Z[[q]]. Since 0 <= a <= b and r >= 0, all indices occurring in the q-Pochhammer symbols are nonnegative, so the definitions make sense.

First rewrite the rational function R_{a,b,r}(q). Because a <= b, we have
(q;q)_{r+b}/(q;q)_{r+a} = (\prod_{t=1}^{r+b} (1-q^t))/(\prod_{t=1}^{r+a} (1-q^t)) = \prod_{t=r+a+1}^{r+b} (1-q^t).
Reindexing with t = r+i gives
(q;q)_{r+b}/(q;q)_{r+a} = \prod_{i=a+1}^{b} (1-q^{r+i}).
Also,
(q;q)_a/(q;q)_b = (\prod_{t=1}^{a} (1-q^t))/(\prod_{t=1}^{b} (1-q^t)) = 1/\prod_{t=a+1}^{b} (1-q^t).
Therefore
R_{a,b,r}(q) = \prod_{i=a+1}^{b} \frac{1-q^{r+i}}{1-q^i}.
When a=b, these are empty products and equal 1, so the same formula is still valid.

Now fix an integer i >= 1. In Z[[q]] one has
(1-q^i) \sum_{m>=0} q^{mi} = \sum_{m>=0} q^{mi} - \sum_{m>=0} q^{(m+1)i} = 1,
because the coefficient of q^0 is 1 and for every positive multiple ni of i the two sums contribute equally and cancel. Hence
(1-q^i)^{-1} = \sum_{m>=0} q^{mi}
inside Z[[q]].

Substituting this inverse into the product formula for R_{a,b,r}(q), and using that the product over i is finite, we obtain in Z[[q]]:
R_{a,b,r}(q) = \prod_{i=a+1}^{b} (1-q^{r+i})(1-q^i)^{-1}
= \prod_{i=a+1}^{b} \left((1-q^{r+i}) \sum_{m>=0} q^{mi}\right)
= F_{a,b,r}(q).
Thus F_{a,b,r}(q) is exactly the formal power-series expansion at q=0 of the rational function R_{a,b,r}(q).

For the final claim, assume R_{a,b,r}(q) belongs to Z[q]. A polynomial, viewed as an element of Z[[q]], is equal to its own power-series expansion at q=0 (with all coefficients above its degree equal to 0). Since the expansion of R_{a,b,r}(q) is F_{a,b,r}(q), we have equality of formal power series
R_{a,b,r}(q) = F_{a,b,r}(q)
in Z[[q]]. Therefore, for every integer j >= 0, the coefficients of q^j are equal:
[q^j] R_{a,b,r}(q) = [q^j] F_{a,b,r}(q).
This proves the lemma.

2. lem_20260329105900_ed0a9993: Let a, b, r be integers with 0 <= a <= b and r >= 0. Define (q;q)_0 := 1 and (q;q)_n := product_{t=1}^n (1 - q^t) for n >= 1, and define R_{a,b,r}(q) := ((q;q)_{r+b} (q;q)_a) / ((q;q)_{r+a} (q;q)_b). For each positive integer d, define M_d(u,v) := |{m in Z : u < m <= v and d divides m}|. Then one has the cyclotomic factorization R_{a,b,r}(q) = product_{d>=1} Phi_d(q)^( M_d(r+a,r+b) - M_d(a,b) ), where Phi_d(q) is the d-th cyclotomic polynomial. Consequently, if R_{a,b,r}(q) belongs to Z[q], then M_d(r+a,r+b) >= M_d(a,b) for every positive integer d.
Let e_d := M_d(r+a,r+b) - M_d(a,b) for each positive integer d. First rewrite the quotient of q-Pochhammer symbols. Since a <= b and r >= 0, we have (q;q)_{r+b}/(q;q)_{r+a} = product_{t=r+a+1}^{r+b} (1 - q^t) and (q;q)_a/(q;q)_b = 1 / product_{t=a+1}^{b} (1 - q^t). Therefore
R_{a,b,r}(q) = product_{i=a+1}^{b} (1 - q^{r+i})/(1 - q^i),
with the empty product equal to 1 when a=b.

Now use the defining factorization of cyclotomic polynomials: for every positive integer N,
q^N - 1 = product_{d | N} Phi_d(q).
For each i with a+1 <= i <= b,
(1 - q^{r+i})/(1 - q^i) = (q^{r+i} - 1)/(q^i - 1) = (product_{d | (r+i)} Phi_d(q)) / (product_{d | i} Phi_d(q)).
Multiplying over i from a+1 to b and collecting equal cyclotomic factors, we get an identity of rational functions
R_{a,b,r}(q) = product_{d >= 1} Phi_d(q)^(A_d - B_d),
where
A_d := |{ i in Z : a < i <= b and d divides (r+i) }|,
B_d := |{ i in Z : a < i <= b and d divides i }|.
If d > r+b, then necessarily d > b as well, so both A_d and B_d are 0. Hence only finitely many exponents are nonzero, so this product is well defined.

It remains to identify A_d and B_d with the M_d counts. The map i -> m := r+i is a bijection from the set counted by A_d onto the set { m in Z : r+a < m <= r+b and d divides m }. Therefore A_d = M_d(r+a,r+b). Also, by definition, B_d = M_d(a,b). Substituting these equalities gives
R_{a,b,r}(q) = product_{d >= 1} Phi_d(q)^( M_d(r+a,r+b) - M_d(a,b) ),
which is the claimed cyclotomic factorization.

For the consequence, assume that R_{a,b,r}(q) belongs to Z[q]. Let I_+ := { d >= 1 : e_d > 0 } and I_- := { d >= 1 : e_d < 0 }. These sets are finite because e_d = 0 for d > r+b. The factorization above can then be written as
R_{a,b,r}(q) = (product_{d in I_+} Phi_d(q)^{e_d}) / (product_{d in I_-} Phi_d(q)^{-e_d}).
Suppose, for contradiction, that I_- is nonempty. Choose D in I_-. Since R_{a,b,r}(q) is actually a polynomial, say P(q) in Z[q], clearing denominators yields the polynomial identity over C,
P(q) product_{d in I_-} Phi_d(q)^{-e_d} = product_{d in I_+} Phi_d(q)^{e_d}.
Now let zeta be a primitive D-th root of unity. By the defining root property of cyclotomic polynomials, Phi_D(zeta)=0, and for every d != D one has Phi_d(zeta) != 0 because zeta is not a primitive d-th root of unity. Evaluating the cleared polynomial identity at q=zeta, the left-hand side is 0 because it contains the factor Phi_D(zeta)^{-e_D} with -e_D > 0, while the right-hand side is nonzero because none of its factors vanish at zeta. This contradiction shows that I_- must be empty.

Thus e_d >= 0 for every positive integer d, i.e.
M_d(r+a,r+b) >= M_d(a,b)
for every positive integer d. This is exactly the stated consequence.

3. lem_20260329105924_711791c7: Let a, b, r, j be integers with 0 <= a <= b, r >= 0, and j >= 0. Put I := {a+1, a+2, ..., b}. Define the formal power series F_{a,b,r}(q) := product_{i in I} ((1 - q^(r+i)) * sum_{m>=0} q^(m i)). Let X_j be the set of pairs (S, lambda) such that S is a subset of I, lambda is a finite multiset of elements of I, |lambda| denotes the sum of the elements of lambda, and |lambda| + sum_{s in S} (r + s) = j. Then [q^j] F_{a,b,r}(q) = sum_{(S,lambda) in X_j} (-1)^(|S|).
Let I = {a+1, a+2, ..., b}. Fix j >= 0. Since a >= 0, every i in I is a positive integer. Hence any term q^(m i) with m > floor(j/i) has degree greater than j, so it cannot contribute to the coefficient of q^j in a product whose other factors also have only nonnegative exponents. Therefore
[q^j] F_{a,b,r}(q) = [q^j] product_{i in I} ((1 - q^(r+i)) sum_{m=0}^{floor(j/i)} q^(m i)).
The right-hand side is now the coefficient of a finite product of finite sums, so we may expand it by the ordinary distributive law.

For each i in I, write
(1 - q^(r+i)) sum_{m=0}^{floor(j/i)} q^(m i) = (sum_{m=0}^{floor(j/i)} q^(m i)) + (- q^(r+i) sum_{m=0}^{floor(j/i)} q^(m i)).

(-1)^(|S|) q^( sum_{i in I} m_i i + sum_{s in S} (r+s) ).
Hence

(The bounds m_i <= floor(j/i) are automatic from the displayed equation, so they do not need to be written separately.)

Now such a family (m_i)_{i in I} is the same thing as a finite multiset lambda of elements of I: namely, lambda contains exactly m_i copies of i for each i in I. Conversely, every finite multiset of elements of I gives such a family of multiplicities. Under this bijection,
|lambda| = sum_{i in I} i m_i.
Therefore, for each fixed S, the inner sum is exactly over those finite multisets lambda of elements of I such that
|lambda| + sum_{s in S}(r+s) = j.
So we get
[q^j] F_{a,b,r}(q) = sum over all subsets S of I of sum over all finite multisets lambda of elements of I with |lambda| + sum_{s in S}(r+s) = j of (-1)^(|S|).
By the definition of X_j, this is exactly
sum_{(S,lambda) in X_j} (-1)^(|S|).
Thus [q^j] F_{a,b,r}(q) = sum_{(S,lambda) in X_j} (-1)^(|S|), as claimed.

Finally, the sum over X_j is finite: if (S,lambda) belongs to X_j, then |lambda| <= j, and since every element of I is at least 1, lambda has at most j elements. Because I is finite, there are only finitely many such multisets lambda, and there are only finitely many subsets S of I. So the right-hand side is well-defined.

4. lem_20260329105947_d7a87760: Let X be a finite set and let w : X -> { -1, +1 } be a sign function. Suppose iota : X -> X satisfies iota(iota(x)) = x for every x in X, w(iota(x)) = -w(x) whenever iota(x) != x, and w(x) = +1 whenever iota(x) = x. Then sum_{x in X} w(x) = |{x in X : iota(x) = x}|. In particular, sum_{x in X} w(x) is a nonnegative integer.
Let F := {x in X : iota(x) = x} be the set of fixed points, and let M := X \ F. Since X is finite, both F and M are finite, and X is the disjoint union F ⊔ M. Therefore
sum_{x in X} w(x) = sum_{x in F} w(x) + sum_{x in M} w(x).

First consider F. By hypothesis, whenever iota(x) = x we have w(x) = +1. Hence every term in the sum over F equals 1, so
sum_{x in F} w(x) = |F|.

Now consider M. If x belongs to M, then iota(x) != x. Also iota(iota(x)) = x, so iota(x) is again in M; thus each x in M belongs to a two-element set {x, iota(x)}. Let
O := { {x, iota(x)} : x in M }.
Each member of O has exactly two elements, because x != iota(x) for x in M. Moreover, O is a partition of M: every x in M lies in {x, iota(x)}, and if two such sets intersect, then they are equal. Indeed, if z lies in both {x, iota(x)} and {y, iota(y)}, then {x, iota(x)} = {z, iota(z)} and also {y, iota(y)} = {z, iota(z)}, so the two sets are equal.

Since O partitions M, we may sum over its blocks:
sum_{x in M} w(x) = sum_{A in O} sum_{x in A} w(x).
For any block A in O, write A = {x, iota(x)} with x in M. Then iota(x) != x, so the sign-reversal hypothesis applies and gives w(iota(x)) = -w(x). Therefore
sum_{y in A} w(y) = w(x) + w(iota(x)) = w(x) - w(x) = 0.
Thus every block contributes 0, and consequently
sum_{x in M} w(x) = 0.

Combining the two parts,
sum_{x in X} w(x) = |F| + 0 = |F| = |{x in X : iota(x) = x}|.
This proves the stated identity. In particular, the sum is the cardinality of a finite set, hence a nonnegative integer.

For each positive integer d, define M_d(u,v) := |{m in Z : u < m <= v and d divides m}|, and assume M_d(r+a,r+b) >= M_d(a,b) for every positive integer d. Let X_j be the set of pairs (S, lambda) such that S is a subset of I, lambda is a finite multiset of elements of I, |lambda| denotes the sum of the elements of lambda, and |lambda| + sum_{s in S} (r + s) = j. Then there exists an involution iota_j : X_j -> X_j such that: (1) if iota_j(S,lambda) = (S',lambda') != (S,lambda), then |S'| is congruent to |S| + 1 modulo 2; and (2) if iota_j(S,lambda) = (S,lambda), then |S| is even.
Let
Q(q) := product_{i=a+1}^b ((1 - q^(r+i)) / (1 - q^i)).
For the fixed j, write
E_j := { (S, lambda) in X_j : |S| is even }
and
O_j := { (S, lambda) in X_j : |S| is odd }.
Because I is finite and every element of I is a positive integer, there are only finitely many multisets lambda with |lambda| <= j; hence X_j, E_j, and O_j are finite.

First, the coefficient of q^j in Q(q) is exactly |E_j| - |O_j|. Indeed, for each i in I,
(1 - q^(r+i)) / (1 - q^i) = (1 - q^(r+i)) * sum_{m>=0} q^(mi).
When we expand the whole product, choosing the term -q^(r+i) from the numerator factor means that i is placed into S, while choosing q^(mi) from the geometric-series factor means that lambda contains i with multiplicity m. The total exponent is then
sum_{s in S} (r+s) + |lambda|,
and the sign is (-1)^|S|. Therefore the coefficient of q^j is
sum_{(S,lambda) in X_j} (-1)^|S| = |E_j| - |O_j|.

Next, Q(q) is a polynomial. Using the cyclotomic factorization 1 - q^m = product_{d|m} Phi_d(q), the exponent of Phi_d(q) in Q(q) is
|{ i in I : d divides (r+i) }| - |{ i in I : d divides i }|.
Since I = {a+1,...,b}, this exponent is exactly
M_d(r+a,r+b) - M_d(a,b),
which is >= 0 by hypothesis. Hence every cyclotomic exponent in Q(q) is nonnegative, so Q(q) belongs to Z[q].

Now set N := r + a + b. By the standard product formula for Gaussian q-binomial coefficients,
[N choose k]_q = (q;q)_N / ((q;q)_k (q;q)_(N-k)).
Therefore
[N choose b]_q / [N choose a]_q
= ((q;q)_a (q;q)_(N-a)) / ((q;q)_b (q;q)_(N-b))
= ((q;q)_a (q;q)_(r+b)) / ((q;q)_b (q;q)_(r+a))
= Q(q),
because N-a = r+b and N-b = r+a.

We have just shown that this quotient is a polynomial. Applying the allowed Gaussian-quotient positivity statement with n = N, k = b, and l = a, it follows that every coefficient of Q(q) is nonnegative. In particular, the coefficient of q^j is nonnegative. By the first paragraph, this says
|E_j| - |O_j| >= 0,
so |E_j| >= |O_j|.

Since E_j and O_j are finite and |E_j| >= |O_j|, choose an injection f : O_j -> E_j. Define iota_j : X_j -> X_j by
- if x in O_j, set iota_j(x) := f(x);
- if x is in the image f(O_j), set iota_j(x) := f^{-1}(x);
- if x in E_j \ f(O_j), set iota_j(x) := x.
This is well-defined because f is injective, and clearly iota_j^2 = id_{X_j}; so iota_j is an involution.

If iota_j(S,lambda) = (S',lambda') != (S,lambda), then one of the two elements lies in O_j and the other lies in E_j, so |S'| and |S| have opposite parity. Equivalently,
|S'| ≡ |S| + 1 mod 2.
If iota_j(S,lambda) = (S,lambda), then (S,lambda) lies in E_j, so |S| is even.

Thus there exists an involution iota_j : X_j -> X_j with properties (1) and (2).
